{{Short description|Non-convergence in Fourier analysis}}
{{more citations needed|date=January 2008}}

In mathematics, the '''Pinsky phenomenon''' is a result in [[Fourier analysis]].<ref>{{Cite journal
| volume = 27
| issue = 3
| pages = 565–605
| last = Taylor
| first = Michael E. | authorlink = Michael E. Taylor
| title = The Gibbs phenomenon, the Pinsky phenomenon, and variants for eigenfunction expansions
| journal = Communications in Partial Differential Equations
| year = 2002
| doi = 10.1081/PDE-120002866
| s2cid = 122314504
}}</ref> This  phenomenon was discovered by [[Mark Pinsky]] of [[Northwestern University]]. It involves the spherical inversion of the [[Fourier transform]].
The phenomenon involves a lack of convergence at a point due to a discontinuity at boundary.
This lack of convergence in the Pinsky phenomenon happens far away from the boundary of the discontinuity, rather than at the discontinuity itself seen in the [[Gibbs phenomenon]]. This non-local phenomenon is caused by a lensing effect.

==Prototypical example==
Let a function ''g''(''x'') = 1 for |''x''|&nbsp;<&nbsp;''c'' in 3 dimensions, with ''g''(''x'') = 0 elsewhere. The jump at |''x''| = ''c'' will cause an oscillatory behavior of the spherical partial sums, which prevents convergence at the center of the ball as well as the possibility of Fourier inversion at ''x'' = 0. Stated differently, spherical partial sums of a [[Fourier integral]] of the [[indicator function]] of a [[ball (mathematics)|ball]] are divergent at the center of the [[ball (mathematics)|ball]] but convergent elsewhere to the desired indicator function.  This prototype example was coined the ”Pinsky phenomenon” by [[Jean-Pierre Kahane]], CRAS, 1995.

==Generalizations==
This prototype example can be suitably generalized to Fourier integral expansions in higher dimensions, both in [[Euclidean space]] and other non-compact rank-one [[symmetric space]]s.
Also related are [[eigenfunction]] expansions on a [[geodesic]] ball in a rank-one symmetric space, but one must consider boundary conditions. Pinsky and others also represent some results on the [[asymptotic]] behavior of the [[Fejér kernel|Fejér approximation]] in one dimension, inspired by work 
of Bump, [[Persi Diaconis]], and J.&nbsp;B.&nbsp;Keller.
